title: He Gave Up the Patent Fees and Got American Homes Online Through Cable TV
dek: In 1991, an Iranian-born engineer used the coaxial cable already in place to move data both ways in and out of homes, then donated the technology royalty-free to the telecom industry to become a global standard — he could have made billions from it.
why: Medium information density, but it has a complete chain of ‘technology rejected → build your own company → field trial and error → give up the patent’, suited to anyone interested in infrastructure innovation and open-source motives.
who: Founders and engineers interested in infrastructure innovation, open-source motives, and 1990s internet history, especially those working on hardware or the network layer.

points.h: The idea everyone called him crazy for
points.body: In 1991, Ruzbe Yassini and his team used the coaxial cable already laid across America for cable TV to move data both ways in and out of homes, connecting millions of American households to the internet for the first time. He recalls that bankers, the cable TV industry and every investor reacted the same way: you're crazy, nobody will solve these problems; and even if you do, nobody will care — who wants to connect data at home? The absurdity of that judgment is that they were betting ‘homes don't need data’, while Yassini was betting ‘the infrastructure is already there’.

points.h: Two jobs pieced together the technical route
points.body: Yassini's technical instinct didn't come from nowhere. From 1981 to 1986 at General Electric he learned how television systems and cable TV systems work, how audio and video entertainment works; around 1987 at a high-speed data company called Proteant he learned how high-speed data works. His judgment was: put high-speed data onto cable TV infrastructure. In the 1980s many people assumed a whole new set of wires had to be laid, and the dream was fiber to the home — fiber itself was fine, the problem was cost. At the time about 56 million American households were already connected to cable TV, and digging new trenches, pulling new cable and hiring people would have been extraordinarily expensive.

points.h: The hardest part was making data travel back
points.body: Coaxial cable had until then only been used to send cable TV programming one way into homes, and the hard part was getting data to travel back. Yassini told the founder of the company he was at, and the reaction was: if anyone wanted to do this, they'd have done it already; besides, who cares about homes being connected? Who would use a computer and a network at home? After being rejected he didn't stop, first getting the system running at Rock Island Arsenal, an army base. But the real question was: could this thing run not just in the closed network of a government building, but in homes across thousands of villages, towns and cities?

points.h: The first field test failed completely
points.body: In 1990 he founded his own company and found real homes to test. A local commercial and residential cable TV company in the small Massachusetts town of Stowe was willing to give them a channel to try. The first trial found that residential cable TV lines were so noisy they couldn't even find their own signal. He says they didn't call it signal-to-noise ratio, they called it noise-to-signal ratio, the situation was very horrible, and they failed badly on residential cable. This was the most dangerous moment of the whole technical route: running in the lab and on a base didn't mean it could run in real homes.

After solving the problems one by one, they ran a second test: sending a file from a residential address to the company office, always the same image of a pigeon in flight. Once the file transfer started, everything ran perfectly over the old residential cable, and the team excitedly called him, shouting ‘the pigeon is now flying over that network infrastructure’. That image is the most concrete success signal in the whole episode — not a metric being hit, but a pigeon flying from a home to the office.

Once the technology worked, he didn't go make billions; he licensed the technology to the telecom industry royalty-free. He says people often ask: don't entrepreneurs always make money first and then donate a little to become famous? Why did he do it the other way around? His explanation: he comes from a region where most problems since the invention of oil have come from that middle stretch of land, and he always thought that if there were a remote communication system that could do healthcare, education and other good things, it could reduce dependence on oil, both protecting the planet from pollution and giving the people of that region freedom to enjoy everything a democratic society brings. So he believed donating the technology royalty-free and making it a global standard was the cornerstone of his vision at the time.

After the royalty-free licensing made the technology a standard, Yassini went on to build a mass-market cable modem for home use. By 1995 his modems held a considerable share of the American market; just one year later his company was acquired for tens of millions of dollars. The whole thing started with 13 people plus 7 advisors, 20 people pushing a vision into execution, and then pushing execution into a tool usable in the home.
